item.title: Fake GitHub Security Tools Infected Over 2,000 Windows Machines
item.description:
More than 2,000 Windows machines have been taken over by the security tools their owners cloned from GitHub and built themselves. The people getting hit are cybersecurity professionals, paid to stop exactly this. The fake repositories have been going up for two years, and some are still online today.

The trap works the way these people already work. A researcher needs a scanner, a reverse proxy, a script to clean up the output of another tool. They search GitHub, they find a repository that looks right, they clone it, and they build it. That last step is the one that ends it. The moment they build it, or even only open it, the machine is no longer theirs.

Doctor Web pulled the malware apart on November 5, 2026, and named the loader that runs it all Trojan.Loader.3261. The researchers found the malicious code hidden inside three kinds of project files, and each one fires in a different way.

In a Visual Studio C# project, the trap sits in the .csproj file as a pre-build event. A pre-build event is a command the project runs before the compiler even starts, meant for ordinary things like copying a file or stamping a version number. Here it runs a PowerShell command instead, the second the developer hits build.

In the same project there is a second file, the .suo, that holds another PowerShell command. The .suo lives in a hidden .vs folder that a developer rarely opens and that a file manager hides by default. In October 2023, Zhiniang Peng of Sangfor showed that a crafted .suo file can run code when a Visual Studio solution is simply opened, before anything is compiled at all. Microsoft did not treat that as a vulnerability. It said opening a project from an untrusted source is an insecure operation, and that users should turn on the trust settings to protect themselves.

The third path is for the Python and Go versions of these fake tools. There the malicious code is pushed far off the right edge of the file, behind a long run of whitespace, so a developer scrolling through the source sees a blank line and reads straight past it.

Once any of those three fires, a PowerShell script lands on disk and reaches out. It pulls an encrypted link from the attackers’ own servers and, alongside them, from ordinary places: YouTube, Telegram, Google Docs, GitCode and Pastebin. Traffic to those everyday sites looks like nothing on a corporate network. The decrypted link downloads an archive called Quixo.7z, which unpacks into a folder dressed up to look like a Windows photo component.

Inside that archive sits Microsoft.exe, and this is the program that does the damage. Doctor Web found it at version 1.4.5. It is built with Electron, the same toolkit behind many everyday desktop apps, so on the machine it looks like one more normal program. Then it goes after the defenses, one by one. It turns off Windows Defender, User Account Control, the pop-up warnings, System Restore and the Volume Shadow Copy Service that backups lean on.

The loader goes further. It puts RegAsm.exe and dwm.exe on Defender’s exclusion list, so the code it later hides in them is never scanned. It tries to remove three security products, McAfee, ESET and Malwarebytes. And it rewrites the Windows hosts file so the machine can no longer even reach the websites of antivirus makers. When it is done, the machine has no guard left and no way to call out for a new one.

Getting that code to run without setting off an alarm is a job on its own, and the loader has a trick for each guard. It makes its own process look like a child of explorer.exe, the program behind your desktop, so it passes for something Windows started itself. It flips a setting in the registry to slip past Smart App Control, the check that is meant to block untrusted apps.

Security tools work by hooking into Windows and watching what runs through. So the loader quietly pulls those hooks back out. It reads a clean copy of ntdll.dll, a core Windows file, straight from disk and uses it to undo them. It calls Windows directly, underneath the layer where the watching happens, a move known as Halo’s Gate. And it switches off two parts of Windows, called ETW and AMSI, that would otherwise let a scanner watch what is running. The payloads end up tucked inside trusted programs like RegAsm.exe and dwm.exe.

What it drops is built to pay off in more than one way. The loader installs two separate copies of the AsyncRAT backdoor. They are identical except for the network port each one uses, and the researchers say this could let two operators hold the same machine at once, each through its own port. One infected computer, two operators, neither of them the person who bought it.

Alongside the backdoors comes a clipboard stealer. It watches for a cryptocurrency wallet address being copied and swaps in the attackers’ address, so money meant for one wallet lands in another. On each swap it grabs a screenshot and sends it to a Telegram bot, together with the title of the active window, the username and the machine’s IP address.

The last piece is an information stealer, and what it goes after is exactly what sits on a security professional’s laptop. It checks first whether it is running in a sandbox or a virtual machine. If the coast is clear, it collects browser data, the saved sites and passwords in FileZilla, the MobaXterm.ini file full of saved SSH sessions, Total Commander’s FTP logins, VPN settings, messenger files, gaming accounts and Discord tokens. All of it gets packed up and sent out through the Telegram bot. These are the keys to other people’s networks, held by the people paid to defend them.

The campaign began somewhere else entirely. In the early days the fake repositories were bots and cheats for crypto games, including one built around the Telegram game Catizen, going after people chasing a quick token. For readers without the right setup, some of those repositories even walked them through installing Visual Studio and cloning the project, step by step.

At some point the operators turned toward a richer target and started dressing the same malware up as scanning tools, security testing tools and log analysis scripts. The researchers also found a component that is not finished yet, built to install the loader as a Windows service and re-download it if it is ever removed. Whoever runs this is still building.

These repositories are still out there. Checking the ones in Doctor Web’s published indicators this morning, two days after the report, several were still live. One is advertised as a lightweight script to parse and clean up the output of Fscan, a network scanner with nearly 15,000 stars that security testers rely on. Another lifts its description straight from a genuine open-source tool, so it reads as legitimate at a glance. Two of the nine example repositories now return a 404. The rest were still there.

Researchers have run into this same toolkit before. In June 2025, Trend Micro wrote about a campaign it called Water Curse, with at least 76 GitHub accounts pushing fake penetration-testing tools. It used the very same parts: a pre-build event in a .csproj, an Electron app, a scheduled task that relaunches a Microsoft.exe on a timer, code slipped into RegAsm.exe, and Telegram used the same way to carry the stolen data out.

The overlap runs down to the internal file names. Trend Micro found the same hidden modules in 2025, boot_f, kernel_f and thread_f, and could only guess what some of them did. Doctor Web has now taken the same pieces apart. The file names and the methods line up that closely, but that does not prove the same people are behind both.

In security, working out who did it is one of the hardest problems there is. Tools get shared, sold and copied, and the same tricks can belong to one group or to several using the same playbook. What we can be sure of is how the malware works, not whose hands are on the keyboard.

Hiding code behind a long stretch of whitespace is older still. In February 2025, Kaspersky wrote up GitVenom, hundreds of fake GitHub projects where the Python payload sat behind about 2,000 tab characters. One of the attackers’ wallets took in roughly 5 BTC, about 485,000 dollars at the time.

Handing a security researcher a Visual Studio project with a trap inside is an old idea. In January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group described a campaign it put down to a government-backed group in North Korea. The attackers made contact, offered to work together on research, and sent over a project with a malicious DLL wired to run through the build events. That is Google’s read on that 2021 case, and nothing here ties it to the GitHub campaign running now.

After that, Microsoft added a trust setting you can switch on, one that makes you approve a project from an untrusted source before it opens. It stays off unless you turn it on yourself. A warning that appears on its own came later, in Visual Studio 2022 version 17.12 from November 2024, and only when the file carries a Mark of the Web, the little tag Windows puts on anything you download. Code pulled straight down with git clone often has no such tag, so no warning shows up.

So the defense comes down to a habit. Before opening a cloned project, look inside the project file itself. In a Visual Studio project, open the .csproj in a plain text editor and check for a pre-build event you did not expect:

1
2
3

<Target Name="PreBuild" BeforeTargets="PreBuildEvent">
  <Exec Command="powershell -enc ..." />
</Target>

A line like that, calling PowerShell or a script before the code even compiles, has no legitimate reason to sit in a tool you cloned minutes ago. Older projects tuck the same command inside a plain <PreBuildEvent> tag, so look for either. Delete the hidden .vs folder before you open the solution, so a planted .suo cannot run. Scroll Python and Go files all the way to the right, past where the text seems to end. And do all of it on a throwaway virtual machine with a clean snapshot, never on the laptop that holds your working keys. Doctor Web published the full list of indicators, the four attacker domains, the IP addresses and the file hashes, in its malware-iocs repository, and its products detect and remove this family.

item.title: Windows Paint Had a Code Execution Hole and the Fix Microsoft Named Never Reached the Store
item.description:
One crafted file opened in Paint could run an attacker’s code. In all 6 countries checked, the Store had no safe Paint. Auto-updates did not help. The fix Microsoft named on October 13 never got there.

On November 5, a Windows 11 PC with automatic app updates switched on in the Microsoft Store showed no update for Paint. Its owner assumed Paint was fine, and then looked up the version in the app’s settings.

Paint was running version 11.2603.251.0. According to Microsoft’s own documentation, only 11.2609.401.0 or newer was safe. The PC belonged to the editor of a Windows news site.

Microsoft tracks the hole as CVE-2026-83844. A program keeps the data it works with in blocks of memory, and each block has a fixed size. When Paint opens a picture, it reads what is in the file into such a block and works from there. Reading past the end of that block, into memory that was never meant for it, is called an out-of-bounds read. A file made for exactly that makes Paint do it, and according to Microsoft that can end with an attacker’s code running on your PC.

Microsoft’s own example of an attack is ordinary. Someone talks you into downloading a specially crafted file from a website, and you open it. Microsoft does not say which file type does it. The person who found the hole reported it anonymously.

Microsoft published the hole on October 13, the second Tuesday of the month, the day it releases its monthly security updates. On the same page it named the Paint version that fixed it: 11.2605.91.0.

That version never showed up in the Store or anywhere else.

On October 30, someone asked on Microsoft’s own question and answer forum where 11.2605.91.0 could be downloaded. The newest Paint they could get was 11.2605.81.0. 40 people clicked that they had the same question. The only answer came from another user, who did not think the version existed and guessed it was a typo.

Somewhere before November 4, Microsoft changed the number. In the security data Microsoft publishes for scanners and IT tools, the fixed version was now 11.2609.401.0. Microsoft added no note about the change to the page. And that version was not in the Store either.

The Store’s own product catalog shows why the update did not come. On November 5 at 03:34 UTC, Brian Vitko, who builds device management software at the company RFF, asked that catalog which Paint packages it had. He asked for six countries: the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Australia, India and Singapore. All six gave the same answer. The newest Paint was 11.2605.81.0. That is below the fix, so the Store had nothing better to install.

His two Windows 11 lab machines showed the same thing. Paint was on 11.2605.81.0 for each user, and as far as the Store was concerned, both machines were up to date. He then ran the update scan that company management tools use to push Store updates to their PCs, and watched Paint for four minutes. It stayed where it was.

The Windows 11 PC from the start of this post was further behind still. Its 11.2603.251.0 sat two releases below even the Store’s newest, while automatic updates were on.

Windows Update could not help here either. On a Windows PC, most fixes come through Windows Update, and Microsoft releases them on that second Tuesday of each month. The Paint app you open on Windows 11 comes from the Microsoft Store, in the same way as an app you install yourself, and only the Store updates it.

Microsoft’s own label for this fix says you have to do something yourself. Installing the October update for Windows 11 did not fix Paint. A PC that is fully up to date through Windows Update can still carry the old Paint.

On October 13, Microsoft gave the hole a score of 8.1 out of 10 and described it as an attack over the network, with no sign-in and no click from you. According to the first version of the page, an attacker could do it by sending a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network.

That made little sense for a drawing program. Paint does not listen on the network. The developer who tested the Store said exactly that in an interview, and added that the sentence may simply have been Microsoft’s standard FAQ wording.

On November 7, Microsoft lowered the score to 7.0. The attack is now local, and you have to do something yourself: open the file. In the revision history, Microsoft called it an informational change only.

That score is a CVSS score, a number from 0 to 10 that says how bad a hole is. Behind the number sits a short code that describes the attack. In October the code said the attack came over the network and needed nothing from you. Now it says the attack is local, AV:L, and that you have to do something yourself, UI:R. The attack runs on your own PC, and only after you open the file.

Microsoft still calls it remote code execution. According to its new explanation, the word remote is about where the attacker sits, and that can be anywhere.

The first version is still out there. Articles written before November 7 describe an attack over the network, with no sign-in and no help from the user, and some headlines still call it a no-click bug. A story about this hole from last week may still describe the old version, the one Microsoft took back.

This is the second hole in Paint in two months.

On September 8, Microsoft published CVE-2026-70586, also in Paint. It rated that one Critical, with a score of 8.8. In that hole, Paint could write more data into a block of memory than fits, and the rest landed in the memory next to it. That is called a heap-based buffer overflow. Here too, the attack needs you to open a specially crafted file from the attacker.

This time the fix came inside Windows itself, through the normal monthly Windows update, for Windows 11, Windows Server 2012 up to 2025 and the Windows 10 versions that still get security updates. Windows 10 lost its normal support on October 14, 2025, so a home PC on Windows 10 only got this fix through Extended Security Updates.

Notepad went the same way, step by step. On February 10, Microsoft fixed a hole in it, CVE-2026-20841. The attack was a link inside a Markdown file. Clicking that link could make the app start other programs without checking them first, through so-called unverified protocols. Those could load and run files from your PC or from the internet. The fix was version 11.2512.26.0, and it came through the Store as well.

Reports at publication gave the hole a score of 8.8, as an attack over the network. Two days later, on February 12, Microsoft updated the score. Today it stands at 7.8, local, and the user has to open the file and click the link. On March 12, a month after the first fix, Microsoft wrote that it had released new updates to comprehensively address the hole. That is almost the same sentence it used for Paint on November 6.

Windows installs Store apps per user. Each account on a PC has its own copy of Paint: yours, your partner’s, the children’s, an extra admin account someone made once and then forgot. On top of that, Windows keeps a spare copy, called the provisioned copy, that it hands to each new account. A check of only your own account misses the others.

The spare copy counts too. When someone makes a new account on that PC, for a new colleague or for a child who gets a login of their own, Windows gives that account Paint from the spare copy. An old spare copy means the new account starts with the old Paint.

At work it can go one step further. A company can switch off the Store on its PCs with a policy called Turn off the Store application. One Microsoft page says app updates need the Store.

Another Microsoft page says Store apps keep updating on their own, and that PCs managed with Intune can still install them. Microsoft contradicts itself here, so on those PCs the IT department has to check whether Paint got the fix, with the same check further down in this post.

The fix arrived on November 6. At 04:14 UTC, the same catalog question returned 11.2609.401.0 for the United States, the United Kingdom and Germany. Microsoft added that version to its page the same day. The developer’s test machine had already picked it up on its own through Store auto-update, for the signed-in user and for the spare copy. That was 24 days after the hole was published.

A Microsoft spokesperson said that the update is available through the Store and that customers with automatic Store updates are already protected. Microsoft has not seen the hole used in attacks and thinks an attack is less likely. It says an attacker has to know the target PC very well, and even then the attack may fail.

CISA, the US cyber defense agency, gave its own view in the public record of the hole. It has not seen attacks either, and it rates the technical damage of a working attack as total.

The official records were late too. The public CVE record kept listing the version that never reached the Store until late on November 7. NVD, the US vulnerability database, still lists the hole as under analysis and has not yet added the version check that scanners look for. A scanner that only reads NVD has nothing to compare your Paint against.

What you can do on your own PC:

  • → Open Paint, go to Settings, and look at the version under About. 11.2609.401.0 or higher has the fix
  • → In the Microsoft Store, open Downloads and check for updates
  • → Keep automatic app updates on: in the Store, go to your profile, then Store settings, then App updates
  • → Check all copies of Paint on one PC in Windows PowerShell, opened as administrator:
1
2

Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers -Name Microsoft.Paint | Select-Object Version, @{ n = 'Users'; e = { $_.PackageUserInformation.UserSecurityId.Username -join ', ' } }
Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online | Where-Object DisplayName -eq 'Microsoft.Paint' | Select-Object Version

The first line lists each user’s copy of Paint, with the account it belongs to. The second line shows the spare copy for new accounts. Keep the -AllUsers in the first line. Without it, you only see your own copy. Anything below 11.2609.401.0 still has the hole.

  • → See which Paint the Store offers in your country. Change market=US to your own country code, for example NL or DE:
1
2

$u = 'https://displaycatalog.mp.microsoft.com/v7.0/products?bigIds=9PCFS5B6T72H&market=US&languages=en-us'
[regex]::Matches((Invoke-WebRequest $u -UseBasicParsing).Content, 'Microsoft\.Paint_([\d.]+)_') | ForEach-Object { [version]$_.Groups[1].Value } | Sort-Object -Unique | Select-Object -Last 1

It prints the newest Paint the Store has for that country. 11.2609.401.0 or later means the fix is there, and a Store update will install it.

  • → At work, ask IT whether Paint reached 11.2609.401.0 on the PCs where the Store is switched off

Microsoft published the hole on October 13, the second Tuesday of the month, the day it releases its monthly security updates. On the same page it named the Paint version that fixed it: 11.2605.91.0.

That version never showed up in the Store or anywhere else.

On October 30, someone asked on Microsoft’s own question and answer forum where 11.2605.91.0 could be downloaded. The newest Paint they could get was 11.2605.81.0. 40 people clicked that they had the same question. The only answer came from another user, who did not think the version existed and guessed it was a typo.

Somewhere before November 4, Microsoft changed the number. In the security data Microsoft publishes for scanners and IT tools, the fixed version was now 11.2609.401.0. Microsoft added no note about the change to the page. And that version was not in the Store either.

The Store’s own product catalog shows why the update did not come. On November 5 at 03:34 UTC, Brian Vitko, who builds device management software at the company RFF, asked that catalog which Paint packages it had. He asked for six countries: the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Australia, India and Singapore. All six gave the same answer. The newest Paint was 11.2605.81.0. That is below the fix, so the Store had nothing better to install.

His two Windows 11 lab machines showed the same thing. Paint was on 11.2605.81.0 for each user, and as far as the Store was concerned, both machines were up to date. He then ran the update scan that company management tools use to push Store updates to their PCs, and watched Paint for four minutes. It stayed where it was.

The Windows 11 PC from the start of this post was further behind still. Its 11.2603.251.0 sat two releases below even the Store’s newest, while automatic updates were on.

Windows Update could not help here either. On a Windows PC, most fixes come through Windows Update, and Microsoft releases them on that second Tuesday of each month. That made little sense for a drawing program. Paint does not listen on the network. The developer who tested the Store said exactly that in an interview, and added that the sentence may simply have been Microsoft’s standard FAQ wording.

That score is a CVSS score, a number from 0 to 10 that says how bad a hole is. Behind the number sits a short code that describes the attack. In October the code said the attack came over the network and needed nothing from you. Now it says the attack is local, AV:L, and that you have to do something yourself, UI:R. The first version is still out there. Articles written before November 7 describe an attack over the network, with no sign-in and no help from the user, and some headlines still call it a no-click bug. A story about this hole from last week may still describe the old version, the one Microsoft took back.

This is the second hole in Paint in two months.

The fix was version 11.2512.26.0, and it came through the Store as well.

On March 12, a month after the first fix, Microsoft wrote that it had released new updates to comprehensively address the hole. That is almost the same sentence it used for Paint on November 6.

Windows installs Store apps per user. Each account on a PC has its own copy of Paint: yours, your partner’s, the children’s, an extra admin account someone made once and then forgot. On top of that, Windows keeps a spare copy, called the provisioned copy, that it hands to each new account. A check of only your own account misses the others.

The spare copy counts too. When someone makes a new account on that PC, for a new colleague or for a child who gets a login of their own, Windows gives that account Paint from the spare copy. An old spare copy means the new account starts with the old Paint.

At work it can go one step further. A company can switch off the Store on its PCs with a policy called Turn off the Store application. One Microsoft page says app updates need the Store.

Another Microsoft page says Store apps keep updating on their own, and that PCs managed with Intune can still install them. Microsoft contradicts itself here, so on those PCs the IT department has to check whether Paint got the fix, with the same check further down in this post.

Microsoft added that version to its page the same day. The developer’s test machine had already picked it up on its own through Store auto-update, for the signed-in user and for the spare copy. That was 24 days after the hole was published.

A Microsoft spokesperson said that the update is available through the Store and that customers with automatic Store updates are already protected. Microsoft has not seen the hole used in attacks and thinks an attack is less likely. It says an attacker has to know the target PC very well, and even then the attack may fail.

CISA, the US cyber defense agency, gave its own view in the public record of the hole. It has not seen attacks either, and it rates the technical damage of a working attack as total.

The official records were late too. The public CVE record kept listing the version that never reached the Store until late on November 7. NVD, the US vulnerability database, still lists the hole as under analysis and has not yet added the version check that scanners look for. A scanner that only reads NVD has nothing to compare your Paint against.

  • → Open Paint, go to Settings, and look at the version under About. 11.2609.401.0 or higher has the fix
  • → In the Microsoft Store, open Downloads and check for updates
  • → Keep automatic app updates on: in the Store, go to your profile, then Store settings, then App updates
  • → Check all copies of Paint on one PC in Windows PowerShell, opened as administrator:
1
2

Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers -Name Microsoft.Paint | Select-Object Version, @{ n = 'Users'; e = { $_.PackageUserInformation.UserSecurityId.Username -join ', ' } }
Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online | Where-Object DisplayName -eq 'Microsoft.Paint' | Select-Object Version

1
2

$u = 'https://displaycatalog.mp.microsoft.com/v7.0/products?bigIds=9PCFS5B6T72H&market=US&languages=en-us'
[regex]::Matches((Invoke-WebRequest $u -UseBasicParsing).Content, 'Microsoft\.Paint_([\d.]+)_') | ForEach-Object { [version]$_.Groups[1].Value } | Sort-Object -Unique | Select-Object -Last 1

It prints the newest Paint the Store has for that country. 11.2609.401.0 or later means the fix is there, and a Store update will install it.

item.title: Unlock Cars From a License Plate
item.description:
A photo of your license plate could open your car and start its engine from far away. The car’s locks had nothing to do with it. The way in was an admin password the carmaker had left in its own files.

Two security researchers, Shubham Shah and Sam Curry, spent time earlier this year on the connected-car systems behind two car brands, from two sides. Shah is a co-founder of the Australian security firm Assetnote, and he took the Australian side. Curry has been taking apart car systems for years, and he took the United States. The apps let an owner unlock the doors, start and stop the engine, sound the horn and find the car on a map. Both sign customers in through the same software. That software is where it all fell apart.

Start with what happens when you prove who you are to a car app. You open the app, type your email and password, maybe approve a second step on your phone, and the app gets a token. A token is a short code the server hands back that says this phone may send commands to this car. That sign-in work runs on a server the carmaker owns, built on a product called ForgeRock, now part of Ping Identity. It is an identity platform: one system that holds the customer accounts and decides who gets let in. Get into that one system as an administrator, and you stop being one customer. You become all of them at once.

On the Australian side, Shah started by mapping the carmaker’s web addresses. Big companies run far more than the one site customers see. They park internal tools and test systems on subdomains, the lesser-known addresses that hang off the main domain. While combing through the JavaScript files served from the carmaker’s own telematics domain, he found something that should never leave a developer’s laptop. One of those files, a bundle from an outside vendor, had a working administrator login for the identity server written straight into it. It was meant for a test setup. It worked on the live system too. The accounts of paying customers sat behind a password that was printed in a file the website served to the public.

This was not a sloppy company. Shah found the opposite: they had put a lot of work into firewall rules to block access to the sensitive parts. He respects the hardening, and suspects they knew how bad it was to leave this one system exposed, but that some business reason kept it there anyway. That is worse than a company that never noticed at all.

A web application firewall, or WAF, was supposed to sit in front of that identity server and block outside requests to the sensitive parts before they arrive. It did block the obvious paths. Shah and Curry sat stuck at it for days, until they let an AI model read the identity software’s source code for about six hours. The model found one path, /static, that slipped past the firewall where the others were blocked. The two of them had assumed, as people do, that one blocked path meant all of them were blocked. The server behind the firewall read that same address as a command, and from there the admin login did the rest.

On the United States side, the pair reached a hidden management console on the identity servers, a control panel meant only for the company’s own engineers. It still accepted the default username and password the software ships with. That default is public, and the maker’s own manual says to change it before the system goes live. It had not been changed. From that console Shah set up a scheduled task that ran his own code, which gave them command execution on the production server. Command execution means running programs on the company’s own machine, the one serving its customers, as if you worked there. An administrator on that identity server can read, change or delete a customer record and hand out a fresh session for it, and that is the level of access the two of them now had.

A single lookup, by email address or phone number, handed back the account’s password hash, its PIN hash, the push tokens tied to the owner’s phone, and the person’s full name and mobile number. Push tokens are the identifiers that let a service send notifications to a specific phone. A hash is a one-way scramble of the original value, so the password and the PIN did not come back as readable text. A weak PIN could still be guessed offline later. The push tokens, the number and the name needed no guessing: they sat there in plain form.

Taking over an account did not need the owner’s password at all. Through the admin controls, the researchers changed a chosen account’s email to one they held, then set a new password on it directly. When they signed in through the normal app, the system sent a six-digit verification code to the new email address, which they read. From there the app handed them the same token the owner’s own phone would get. On the owner’s side, nothing changed. Their existing app session stayed logged in while the researchers worked beside it, and once they had the tokens they set the original email back, so the account looked untouched. They could even register a push token of their own, so the alerts a car sends would reach them instead of the owner.

The second step that is meant to protect the account did not help either. In the Australian system, the code or the tap on your phone that normally stands between a stolen password and the account could be skipped through an old sign-in method that should have been retired years ago.

This is the part that reaches your own car in your own driveway. Your car carries a VIN, the vehicle identification number stamped on it at the factory and visible through the windshield. Someone walking past can read it off the glass. In Australia, a plate is enough on its own: it gives you the VIN through the state registration-lookup sites, and the admin tool turned a VIN into the exact account it belonged to. That lookup was a built-in part of the system meant for staff, which is why it answered without complaint. In the United States test, Shah checked a car with its owner standing beside it, then unlocked the doors, started the engine, shut it off and locked it again.

A few things keep this from being a nightmare. These were researchers working with permission. The owner in the test stood beside the car and chose a new password after it was done. The researchers did not name the carmaker in their writeups, because they were asked not to, and they held back the exact web addresses and credentials so others could not follow along. They give no number for how many cars or customers could have been reached, only that it would hit an owner who had the remote features switched on. The response was fast: once they reported it, the carmaker fixed it within about two hours, took down the test code, and changed the exposed passwords. The researchers were given no reward and no public credit for the work.

This is not the first time these two have walked into the car industry through the web instead of through the car. Over the past few years they found ways to reach vehicles from brands like Honda, Nissan, Hyundai and Ford, and later dug into Kia and Subaru. Four years ago, in that same stretch of work, they pulled a staging key out of the JavaScript on a Ferrari dealer web page and used it to reach Ferrari’s production systems. From there they could read, change or delete any customer’s account and change its role, and the dealer back office even handed back a set of live service credentials in plain text. Same mistake, a different brand: a test key left where the public could reach it.

Each time the way in was an account or dealer system, not anything mechanical on the vehicle. The finding keeps coming back the same way. The car itself is usually solid. The website and the app behind it are the way in, because they are built fast, wired to live customer data, and harder to lock down than the thing they control.

A few weeks ago I wrote here about how car apps quietly send your VIN off to advertising and tracking firms. It is the same number, pointed at a different danger. In that story it ties your car to your shopping and your movements. In this one it is the first link in a chain that ends with your doors open and your engine running. The number was never meant to be a secret. It is printed on the glass on purpose. That becomes the trouble when a login system treats something people can read off a parked car as something only the owner should know.

You cannot do much about a carmaker’s server, since that part is on them. What you can do is treat your VIN as more public than the apps pretend. Think twice before feeding it into lookup and valuation sites. And remember that the remote features in a car app are only as safe as the company’s weakest web address. This break-in did not need a cut wire or a scanner held near the door. It needed a laptop, a phone app read line by line, and a login the company forgot to lock. On a modern car, the account behind the app has become the way in, long before the lock on the door.

Sam Curry | Shubham Shah

item.title: Webloc Lets Police Track Phones Through the Ads in Weather Apps and Games
item.description:
Police bought a tool that shows where up to 500 million phones have been over 12 months, without a warrant. The location came out of the ads in weather apps, games and a prayer app. Up to 500 million phones sit in the tool they bought, on sale since 2020.

In 2025, a US firm prepared presentations for police forces in several countries to show what its tracking tool, Webloc, could do. On the screen, it followed people’s phones as they walked down Fifth Avenue in New York, visited the European Central Bank in Frankfurt and came close to the UK Parliament in London. Bloomberg News got hold of those presentations, along with training material and internal documents.

The seller is Penlink, which has made software for American police for decades, mostly to analyze tapped phone calls and internet data gathered during investigations. Webloc comes from Israel. It was built by Cobwebs Technologies, set up in 2015 by three veterans of Israeli special forces, who designed it for counterterrorism. In 2023 both ended up under the same US investment firm, and the sale of Webloc moved to the American side. A license starts at around 100,000 dollars a year.

In April, researchers at Citizen Lab, at the University of Toronto, mapped out what that money buys. They worked from contracts, procurement records and leaked documents, and describe access to records from up to 500 million mobile devices across the globe. In the documents the reporters saw, Webloc shows where a phone has been over the past 12 months, refreshed once an hour. One older US contract mentions three years.

An officer opens a map, draws a shape around a street or a building, and picks a time window. Webloc then lists the phones that were inside. It can show which phones turned up in two different places within the same window. It sends an alert when a phone shows up somewhere new, and it shows where a phone spends its nights and where it spends its days.

That last part is how police get from a phone to a name. A 2021 sales proposal for a police force in Central America puts it plainly: work out who is behind the device, find the home and the workplace, and send officers to the suspect.

To follow a phone, Webloc first has to recognize it, and for that it uses the advertising ID. Your phone has a number made for ads, on Android and on the iPhone. Apps read it so that advertisers can recognize the same phone across different apps and show it ads that fit. On an iPhone, an app has to ask your permission first.

The ad industry calls that number anonymous, because it carries no name and no phone number. A number that shows up at the same address night after night, and at the same office in the morning, still points to one person.

The researchers published what a single Webloc record could hold, as of 2021:

  • → the advertising ID and the IP address
  • → the time, plus GPS coordinates or a location worked out from nearby WiFi
  • → the name of the WiFi network the phone was connected to
  • → the brand, model and operating system of the phone
  • → an estimated home, workplace and most visited places
  • → age, gender, and labels such as parent, traveler or gamer
  • → the apps on the phone, with when each was first and last seen

Webloc’s makers say it now only holds locations tied to a device ID, with no age, gender or interests. The researchers had no way to check that.

A location can reach Webloc in two ways, and the researchers could not say for sure which one it uses today.

The first way runs through the app itself. A developer building a free app often adds ready-made code from an outside firm to show ads or to count users. That code is called an SDK, a software development kit, and it runs inside the app. Allow your weather app to see your location, and the code inside it can read that location too and pass it on to whoever wrote it.

One of those code makers is Start.io. According to the documents, its SDK sits in more than 500,000 apps with more than 25 billion downloads between them, and it claims to reach 2.4 billion devices, 300 million of them in the US. A platform that checks Android apps for trackers found one linked to it in more than 4,400 apps.

Some of the location data in Webloc came from there, according to the documents and former employees. Webloc’s makers deny buying it and say the Israeli developers only ran a trial with that data before the takeover. The SDK maker answers that its contracts limit the data to advertising, that most of it is not precise, and that the download figures are theoretical.

The second way needs no code inside the app at all. When an app has room for an ad, it sends out a request, and advertisers bid on it within a fraction of a second. That request can carry the advertising ID and the location of the phone, and those taking part in the auction get to see it. The stream of data from those auctions is called the bidstream. A data broker that joins in can collect locations from apps it never made a deal with.

That is why app makers often have no idea where their users’ locations end up. Webloc’s makers say their partners collect through their own SDK deals and get consent through the apps, but those partners do not hand over a full list of which apps. The seller itself is listed in California’s register of data brokers, and its own privacy policy says it may get a device’s past locations from other brokers.

item.title: SignDrop Turns the Protection Microsoft Built for Windows Log Files Into SYSTEM Access
item.description:
Nightmare Eclipse, the researcher Microsoft fired, released his 17th exploit since April on Patch Tuesday. There is no patch. It turns Microsoft’s protection against 24 bugs into a way to SYSTEM.

This is the eleventh time I am writing about Nightmare Eclipse. Since April I have followed him through BlueHammer, RedSun, UnDefend, YellowKey, MiniPlasma, RoguePlanet, GreatXML, LegacyHive, ShieldBreak and ShieldCrash. In September he put his own name under them: Abdelhamid Naceri, who worked at the Microsoft Security Response Center until Microsoft fired him. His GitHub account is called MSNightmare, and the bio still says I love Microsoft.

The new one is called SignDrop. It lets an ordinary Windows account become SYSTEM, the highest level of access a Windows machine has. It goes after a protection Microsoft built into Windows itself, meant to end a long run of attacks on a single driver.

He has a habit with dates. ShieldCrash went up on September 8, about two hours after that month’s Patch Tuesday updates. Patch Tuesday is the second Tuesday of the month, when Microsoft ships its security fixes. His first exploit on the new account went up on June 9, also a Patch Tuesday. The code for SignDrop went up on November 10. Patch Tuesday again. Microsoft shipped its November fixes that day, and none of them touches SignDrop. There is no CVE number, the official ID a known flaw gets, and no advisory.

Between September and now there was one more, BigDiskBuster, which I did not write about. It waits until Defender starts an update and then fills the drive with hidden temporary files, so the update runs out of space and fails. Defender stays on the version it already had for as long as the tool keeps interfering. He admitted himself that it was a bit buggy. Researchers at one security firm count sixteen public releases from him between April 3 and SignDrop, and their list leaves it out. Counted with that one, SignDrop is his 17th.

Windows has a built-in service that programs use to keep logs, records of what they did, in a fixed format that survives a crash. It is called the Common Log File System, or CLFS, and the driver behind it is clfs.sys. A driver like this runs in the kernel, the core of Windows.

That driver has been one of the most attacked parts of Windows for years. In August 2024 Microsoft counted 24 CVEs in CLFS over five years. 19 of them came from the same mistake: the driver trusted a field in a log file without checking it. An attacker needed nothing special for that. A log file is a file on disk, and an ordinary user can write a malicious one with the normal Windows file functions and then let the driver read it.

Those bugs were used. CISA, the US cybersecurity agency, keeps a catalog of flaws that attackers have exploited. CLFS appears in it 12 times, and for 7 of those 12 the agency notes that ransomware gangs used them. One of the most recent was CVE-2025-29824 in April 2025. Microsoft tied it to a group it calls Storm-2460. Starting from a standard user account, the attackers used the flaw to get into SYSTEM processes, and Microsoft then saw files encrypted on the machines they hit.

So Microsoft changed its approach. Instead of fixing one field at a time, it started checking who wrote the file. Since the updates of October 28, 2025, for Windows 11 25H2 and Windows Server 2025, CLFS signs the log files it writes. It calculates a code from the contents and a secret key that is unique to each machine, called an HMAC, and stores that code at the end of the file. The key sits in the registry, the central settings database of Windows, where only SYSTEM and administrators can reach it. When CLFS opens a log later, it checks the code. If someone changed the file by hand, the code no longer matches and the driver refuses to read it.

The protection also added a small companion file next to each log, with the extension .cnpf, which CLFS uses to repair the log if it was not closed cleanly. Machines that get the update have 90 days to adapt. During that time the protection runs in learning mode: it adds codes to existing logs and still opens them. After 90 days it switches itself to enforcement on the next boot. The protection costs something too. Microsoft’s own documentation says that writing a record takes about twice as long on average.

Naceri says himself in his writeup that publicly exploited CLFS flaws dropped sharply after the protection arrived.

That companion .cnpf file is where SignDrop gets in.

It starts with things an ordinary user is allowed to do. The user asks CLFS to create a log file, which ends in .blf, and attaches extra containers to it, the files where CLFS keeps the actual records. Each container gets its own .cnpf file. Up to this point CLFS checks access properly and creates the files with the user’s own rights.

The trouble starts when a different process opens that log. CLFS opens the attached containers along with it, and it creates the .cnpf files with the rights of whichever process did the opening. If that process runs as SYSTEM, CLFS creates the file as SYSTEM. It also gives the new file the same access rights as the original file, and the original belonged to the user.

So the exploit needs a process that runs as SYSTEM and can be made to open a file. It uses Windows Defender. Defender has an internal interface for its own signature updates. A standard user can call one function in it, ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, and make Defender open the prepared log. Before that, the exploit sets up redirects in Windows’ internal list of names, so one name points to another location. These are called object manager symbolic links. Because of them, the file Defender creates lands in a place the attacker chose. In a screenshot he added to the repository, Defender’s own process is the one creating the file.

What comes out is a file that Windows created with SYSTEM rights, in a location the attacker picked, with access rights the attacker controls. The exploit puts that file in a Windows folder called ink, names it hid.dll and fills it with its own code. It has already started the On-Screen Keyboard, hidden from view. Then it asks Windows to run a program as administrator.

That request opens the UAC window, the box Windows shows when something asks for administrator rights. The program behind that window, consent.exe, runs as SYSTEM, and with that keyboard active it loads hid.dll from the ink folder. The attacker’s code now runs inside that window itself. It opens a command window running as SYSTEM on the user’s desktop and closes the prompt. So the window that is supposed to guard administrator rights is the one that hands them over.

He also writes that the same trick can turn off any antivirus or EDR product, the security software companies run to watch their computers. It gets around the self-protection those products use against tampering. That wider claim has not been tested.

The protection Microsoft built against two dozen CLFS bugs is now the way in, and switching it off does not help. With the registry value Mode set to 2, an administrator has disabled the protection, and SignDrop has nothing to work with. But then CLFS stops checking log files, and Microsoft’s documentation warns that it will read files that may be damaged or planted by an attacker. Naceri gives the same warning in his writeup: turning the protection off opens the machine to the memory corruption bugs it was built against. His only answer is to wait for a patch from Microsoft.

Two security firms have tested it. Cyderes rebuilt the chain and got a console running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, started from a standard user session. A team at the Korean security firm 78researchlab found that it works too, though not reliably enough to use in an attack.

It also has limits. Defender has to be switched on, because Defender is the process doing the work. And a person at that machine would see it: it ends with a SYSTEM command window open on the desktop of whoever is logged in.

In his writeup he estimates that 80 percent of the world’s Windows installations are vulnerable, and he calls it a guess himself. The numbers do not support it. Microsoft ships the protection SignDrop needs for Windows 11 25H2, Windows 11 26H1 and Windows Server 2025. Windows 10 is not on that list, and neither is Windows 11 24H2. Without a .cnpf file the exploit stops, the researchers who rebuilt the chain found.

In October 2026, Statcounter measured 74.29 percent of Windows desktops on Windows 11 and 25.13 percent still on Windows 10. Even if the Windows 11 share had moved to 25H2 or later without a single exception, the ceiling for desktops is about 74 percent. That is below his 80.

For once, the PCs in scope are the newest ones, the machines that took the October 2025 update and moved on to 25H2 or later. A Windows 10 PC, or a Windows 11 PC that stayed on 24H2, is outside this particular exploit. Holding back updates is no answer, because those machines lack the protection against the kind of CLFS bug that ended up in that catalog 12 times.

Microsoft told a security news site that it is actively investigating the report. According to the company, Defender detects and blocks this attack, and raises an alert when an account jumps to higher rights. It has not seen the exploit used in attacks so far. There is still no CVE. Defender is the program the exploit uses, and according to Microsoft it is also the program that stops it.

The fight between him and Microsoft goes on. On May 27, the same response center he used to work for wrote that putting exploit code for unpatched flaws out in public is never justifiable. In that post it named six of his releases as not responsibly disclosed. In August, at DEF CON, the Pwnie Awards gave Microsoft Lamest Vendor Response for its implied legal threats against him. The README for SignDrop ends by telling people who have a problem with the repository to email Microsoft’s own security address. His own blog has been silent since September 18, and the last post there says a close third party manages it, not him.

The first three exploits I named at the top, each aimed at Defender, turned up in live intrusions after he published them. SignDrop has not been seen in an attack yet. The code is public, though. By November 14, four days after release, the repository had 363 stars and 85 copies made by other users, and at least two security firms had tested it.

What you can check on your own machine:

Press Win+R and type winver. If it says 25H2, 26H1 or newer, or Windows Server 2025, your machine is in scope. Then open a command prompt and read the CLFS mode:

1

reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication" /v Mode
  • → 0 means the protection is enforced, 1 means it is in learning mode. Both fall within what SignDrop targets
  • → 2 means an administrator switched the protection off, 3 is a value Windows sets itself. According to Naceri, neither is vulnerable to SignDrop
  • → Do not set Mode to 2 to get rid of SignDrop. That reopens the class of bugs that put CLFS on the US list of exploited flaws 12 times
  • → Keep Defender on and up to date. According to Microsoft, Defender blocks this exploit
  • → Watch for a SYSTEM shell or console started from a standard user session, for Defender’s process, MsMpEng.exe, creating .cnpf files, and for consent.exe loading a hid.dll from the ink folder
  • → Watch Microsoft’s Security Update Guide for a CVE and a fix

Want to see how a standard user climbs to SYSTEM? Build a Windows 11 VM at home, log in without admin rights, and read that CLFS value yourself. So Microsoft changed its approach. Instead of fixing one field at a time, it started checking who wrote the file. That companion .cnpf file is where SignDrop gets in.

item.title: worse_query Lets iPhone Apps Read Other Apps' Files and Apple's Update Left It Open
item.description:
One app on an iPhone can now read the files of the other apps on that phone, wallet seed phrases included. iOS 27.2.1 does not fix it. The code is public, and Apple has had the report since October 20.

On an iPhone, each app gets a folder of its own for its data. A wallet app keeps its keys and settings there, a chat app keeps its messages and photos there. Another app on the same phone is not allowed to look inside. That separation between apps is called the sandbox.

On Sunday, November 8, a researcher who goes by forcequit published a way around it on GitHub. He calls it worse_query, and he built it together with a second researcher, 0xjohnny. His project page lists iOS 26.0 up to 26.7.2, and iOS 27.2. Those versions run on the iPhone 11 and later.

It is his second sandbox escape. His earlier one, bad_query, dates from August, and its page lists iOS 26.0 up to 26.6.1 and the fourth beta of iOS 27.0. worse_query is its successor. He announced it on X as a zero-day sandbox escape for iOS 26 and 27, again. A zero-day is a hole the maker has not fixed yet.

The project page of worse_query lists the folders it can reach. The data folders of the apps installed on the phone are on that list. So are the folders of app extensions, the small add-ons such as widgets and keyboards that come with an app. The folders of internal system services are on it, and so are the shared folders that apps use to pass data to each other. On iOS 27 it reaches some system folders on top of that.

It gives an app access to the files of other apps and leaves the rest of the phone untouched. The researcher wrote that it will never be used in a jailbreak tool.

The app that uses it needs one thing: an App Group. Apple’s developer documentation describes App Groups as a way for apps from the same development team to share a folder. A developer switches it on in Xcode, the tool for building iPhone apps.

The phone has a system service that keeps track of the app folders and decides which app may open which one. worse_query talks to that service and comes away with access to folders that belong to other apps. The researcher calls it a logic bug: the service does what it was built to do, in an order its makers did not plan for.

Someone asked him on X whether MIE, Apple’s protection against attacks on the phone’s memory, stops it. His answer was no. MIE guards against memory corruption, a program writing or reading where it should not, and this is a logic bug.

The two researchers found the bug in August. The second researcher wrote that on X on November 10, and the source code agrees: the main file was created on August 20, 2026.

The researcher reported it to Apple on October 20. He later posted a screenshot of the report page, which shows it came in at 10:27 AM that day. Under it is a note from the company. It usually reviews reports within seven days, the note says, but this one was taking longer and had been given priority.

According to the researcher, Apple did not start looking at his report until November 9. That was the day after he made the code public.

On that same day, November 9, Apple released iOS 27.2.1 and iOS 26.7.3. The security notes list nine fixes in 27.2.1 and eight in 26.7.3. They cover Bluetooth pairing, AirPlay, iMessage group chats and a compression library.

One fix in 27.2.1 sounds close. It is a flaw in a part of iOS called App Intents, and through it an app may be able to access sensitive user data. Apple credits that one to a different researcher, László Várady, and the notes for 26.7.3 do not have it at all. The words sandbox and App Group do not appear in either set of notes.

On November 10 the researcher behind worse_query wrote on X that it is not patched in iOS 27.2.1. It is not patched in the first beta of iOS 27.3 either. He added that he will update the version list on the project page as soon as it is patched.

On the iOS 27.3 beta it works as well. A developer named Christoph Kolbicz built a file manager on top of worse_query, called WQ Files. Its page lists iOS 27.2.1 as tested. It can browse the folders of other apps, back them up, edit files in them and empty them.

A user running iOS 27.3 beta, build 24C5037i, posted the app’s own log on the file manager’s page when something went wrong. He reported that the cache cleaner did not work. The developer found that the app could not tell which folder belonged to which app. The log itself shows something else: access to other apps’ folders, okay. Sandbox access, okay. The scan found 292 apps, 1,134 extensions and 34 system services, and checked 1,426 folders. The developer added 27.3 to the versions it was tested on.

People install it through AltStore or SideStore, tools that put apps on an iPhone outside the App Store. That is called sideloading.

The researcher himself wrote on X on November 8 that he is not releasing anything for end users. His project page calls the code a proof of concept for developers, a demo that shows the hole exists. It is not useful by itself, the page says. Within days, someone else had built a ready-made app for end users on top of it.

He had not planned to publish worse_query at all. On X he explained that several people had found the same bug on their own months earlier, and someone else had already shown it in public. So he released his own version first. In that same thread he warned against releasing zero-days without telling the maker first and agreeing on a date. Especially, he wrote, when they can easily be used for spyware.

His partner put it plainly on November 10: there is no iOS update that fixes it.

Publishing early may have cost the researcher money. Apple pays researchers through its Security Bounty program. The category for a malicious app on iPhone that escapes the sandbox and gets sensitive user data lists 100,000 dollars. The rules of that program also say that a researcher who makes a hole public before a fix is out gets no reward at all. He wrote that he does not mind losing a possible bounty, because Apple was stalling on his report. On November 11 he wrote that Apple was finally investigating it.

On November 10, the crypto exchange Binance posted a warning on X. A malicious app could read local files from other apps, and that put seed phrases, private keys and login credentials at risk. A seed phrase is the list of words that restores a crypto wallet, and whoever has those words has the wallet. The post was viewed 3.8 million times.

The exchange named three versions: iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1 and 27.2. Those three are not the limit. The researcher’s own range is wider, and the file manager’s log shows it on 27.3 beta.

The exchange’s advice was to delete apps from untrusted sources and to update iOS and the apps on the phone. Deleting unknown apps helps. Updating does not, yet. The second researcher wrote on X that Apple has not patched the bug, that the exchange meant well, and that updating alone will not fix it.

For iOS 26.7.3 the picture is not clear. The researcher’s range stops at 26.7.2 and the file manager asks for 26.7.2 or lower. No public test on 26.7.3 has shown up, and the notes for that release say nothing about the sandbox.

The warning was about apps from outside the App Store. The researcher went further. On November 10 he wrote that worse_query would absolutely be exploitable from an App Store app. An attacker would only have to get through App Review. His partner was more careful: unlikely, but there is a risk that an approved app packs this and gets past the review.

App Review is the check Apple runs before an app goes into the store. Rule 2.5.1 of its guidelines says apps may only use public APIs, the functions Apple offers to developers. worse_query calls functions the company keeps for itself, and that is the kind of thing the review is supposed to catch. Rule 2.5.2 says an app may not read or write data outside its own folder. That is exactly what worse_query does.

The review has missed a sandbox escape before, two months ago.

In September, an app called FomoPeek went through the App Store with a sandbox escape inside. The researcher pointed to it himself on X. The analysis came from SlowMist, a blockchain security firm, together with the security team of OKX. The app presented itself as a read-only tool for watching crypto wallets, and it never asked for a seed phrase.

Version 1.0 went live on August 29 and was clean. Version 1.1 arrived on September 9 with two hidden modules, and version 1.2 kept them on September 12. Those carried eight kernel exploits. The kernel is the core of the operating system. The modules also held code to escape the sandbox and code to decrypt the iPhone’s Keychain, where iOS stores passwords and keys. Version 1.3, on September 17, removed both modules again.

The modules came through the official App Store and carried the same developer signature as the app. To get people to install it, the promotion offered 5 to 7 USDT, a cryptocurrency tied to the US dollar. Users had to sign up with a referral code and keep the app open on a physical iPhone for several minutes. The App Store page said Data Not Collected.

The operators steered the app from a distance through a control server. The attack had an on and off switch on that server. In the researchers’ captures it was switched off. According to the analysis, the operators could turn it on or off and change how often it ran, without a new version of the app. The address of that server sat encrypted in a public file on Bitbucket, a site for hosting code. One edit to that file moved the app to another server. What the app did could change after it was in the store, without a new version going through review.

In their test, the researchers flipped that switch on inside the app on their own isolated test device. The server then sent a list of 19 targets, almost all of them wallet apps, including MetaMask, Trust Wallet, OKX Wallet and SafePal. The folder of Apple Notes was on the list too. The researchers watched the app pack up the notes database and upload it. The attacker’s main wallet address received 579,984.34 USDT.

The app used older kernel exploits that reached up to iOS 26.1. worse_query is a different hole. The case shows that a sandbox escape has already passed the review once, in a crypto app that looked harmless.

On November 12 the researcher put it in proportion himself. App Review does mess up rather often, he wrote. A malicious App Store app could be dangerous, and so could an update to an app that was fine before. He added that it is realistically not something to worry about. He also pointed at a second route. Someone could combine worse_query with a second bug that runs code inside an app that already has an App Group, such as a third-party app. Then no sideloading is needed at all.

So far neither the exchange nor the researchers have reported an attack that used worse_query, and no theft has been linked to it. Apple has not said anything. That is its policy: the company does not comment on security issues until it has investigated them and a fix is out.

What you can do on your own iPhone:

  • → Check your version under Settings, General, About, and install the next iOS update as soon as it comes
  • → Do not install apps from outside the App Store, such as sideloaded or self-signed IPA files, the install files for iPhone apps, from people you do not know
  • → Be careful with new App Store apps from unknown developers, especially crypto tools that pay you to install them and keep them open
  • → Keep your seed phrase off the phone: not in Notes and not as a screenshot
  • → Think a wallet on your iPhone was exposed? Create a new wallet with a new seed phrase on a different device, move your funds there, and sign out of your active login sessions

item.title: Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Sat in Web Servers Since 2023 and Ubuntu's Version Numbers Hid It

About 1.5 million web servers run an Apache version that can let an attacker run code without logging in. Switching on HTTP/2 is enough. One line in its HTTP/2 code has written to the wrong memory since 2023.

Apache HTTP Server runs 20.6 percent of the websites whose web server is known, according to the daily count of W3Techs. The scanning company Censys counts about 166 million web addresses running on it, each a name or IP address with a port. On November 11, the Apache project published an advisory for CVE-2026-119618, the public ID for a flaw in mod_http2, the module that lets Apache speak HTTP/2, and gave it the highest rating it has, critical. The title of the advisory says what it does: heap corruption and remote code execution, in a function called assign_headers().

Remote code execution means that someone on the other side of the internet can make the server run commands of their choosing. For this flaw, an attacker needs nothing more than a server that speaks HTTP/2 and a way to reach it, which for a public website is the reason it exists.

The same scanning company found roughly 1.5 million hosts that announce an Apache version from 2.4.55 to 2.4.70, the range Apache lists as affected. It can read a version on only about 40 percent of the hosts running Apache, so that count only covers the servers that say what they run. About 40 percent of those affected hosts sit in five cloud and hosting networks: Amazon, Google, Hetzner, OVH and DigitalOcean, the places where many websites rent the server they run on.

With the older HTTP/1.1, a browser sends one request at a time over a connection and waits for the answer before it sends the next. HTTP/2 lets the browser send many requests over the same connection at once, each in its own numbered stream, so a page with fifty images does not have to fetch them one after the other. Apache handles that by handing the streams of one connection to several separate lines of work inside the same server process, which run side by side. Those are called worker threads.

A request starts with a few lines that tell the server what the browser wants, such as Host, Content-Type and Content-Length. Those lines are the headers. When a request arrives over HTTP/2, mod_http2 reads them and stores them in a table that belongs to that stream. The worker thread that picks up the request then makes its own copy of that table, and from that moment on the request is supposed to work on the copy.

Inside assign_headers() sits a small rule for one specific case. When a request says it has no body, but does carry a Content-Type header and no Content-Length, Apache adds a Content-Length of zero, so the rest of the server knows that no data will follow. The comment in the source code says exactly that. In Apache 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, the line that adds it writes into the original table instead of the copy:

1

apr_table_setn(req->headers, "Content-Length", "0");

That original lives in memory that the connection manages. As long as the table has room, the extra header fits in. When the table is full and has to grow, the worker thread takes new memory from the connection while other threads of the same connection are busy with their own streams. Nothing makes them wait for each other.

Red Hat, which ships Apache in its own Linux distribution, describes the result as one thread modifying memory that belongs to another thread. When two threads touch the same memory without taking turns, the outcome depends on which one gets there first, and that is called a race condition. Here the race damages the pool of memory the server hands out to itself while it runs, known as the heap. Apache’s advisory says that damage can lead to remote code execution.

The correction the Apache developers wrote changes that one line and nothing else in the file. The value now goes into the request’s own copy, where only that worker thread touches it:

1
2

- apr_table_setn(req->headers, "Content-Length", "0");
+ apr_table_setn(r->headers_in, "Content-Length", "0");

A small program on GitHub triggers the flaw from outside. That kind of program is called a proof of concept, and this one sends an HTTP/2 request that ends right after its headers, with a Content-Type and without a Content-Length. It fills the header table to its limit with 79 ordinary headers plus Host. In the author’s lab, Apache 2.4.70 crashes, and the memory checkers that developers use to catch these errors report corruption. The proof of concept does not show code running.

Red Hat’s page for the CVE says that public research has shown a reliable working attack on a server in its default setup with the HTTP/2 module switched on. Its security bulletin adds that an attacker can trigger the problem reliably with a carefully built series of HTTP/2 requests sent at the same time. Neither page names that research.

The first version with the flaw is Apache 2.4.55, released in January 2023, and the last one is 2.4.70. For the standalone version of the module, distributed separately as mod_h2, Apache lists 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. A server that kept Apache up to date since early 2023 has been carrying the flaw for close to four years.

This is the fifth HTTP/2 flaw on Apache’s list for 2026, and the first one Apache rates critical. The most serious before it was CVE-2026-23918 in May, rated important: a flaw where the server releases the same piece of memory twice, called a double free, with possible remote code execution.

Two teams found this flaw separately. The first report came on October 26 from Anthropic’s OSS Scanner, an opt-in scanner for open-source projects that the company launched on October 8. An AI model writes its reports, and no person checks them before they go out. Apache credits the scanner under the ID ANT-2026-MAPKT6MZ. Eight days later, on November 3, Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported the same flaw. Apache published its advisory on November 11.

The flaw sits in the HTTP/2 module, so it only reaches servers where HTTP/2 is switched on, through h2 or h2c in a setting called Protocols. Servers that only speak HTTP/1.1 are not affected. In Apache’s own documentation, the default for that setting is Protocols http/1.1, so HTTP/2 stays off until an administrator turns it on.

On Debian, turning it on takes one command, sudo a2enmod http2. The configuration file that comes with the module starts with the line Protocols h2 h2c http/1.1. That switches on HTTP/2 over an encrypted connection (TLS), which is h2, and also h2c, which is HTTP/2 over a connection without encryption. Apache’s documentation explains that a site inherits this line from the main server configuration unless it sets a Protocols line of its own. On a fresh Debian install the module is off, so on Debian HTTP/2 is a choice the administrator made, with that one command.

Ubuntu 22.04 runs Apache 2.4.52, and Ubuntu 20.04 runs 2.4.41. Both numbers are older than 2.4.55, the first version Apache lists as affected. Both releases had the flaw anyway, and Ubuntu’s page for this CVE lists a fix for both and gives the reason. Ubuntu copied newer versions of the HTTP/2 module into the older Apache package of its stable releases, which is called backporting. The Apache version number stayed old, while the HTTP/2 code inside it was newer, including the broken line. The version number gave no warning.

An administrator who runs apache2 -v on such a server sees 2.4.52 and finds it below the affected range. Internet scans that sort servers by the version they announce make the same call. An Ubuntu 22.04 server with HTTP/2 switched on does not fall in the range from 2.4.55 to 2.4.70, so it is not in that count of 1.5 million either. Ubuntu 18.04 and older are not affected, according to the same page.

The severity score depends on who gives it. Red Hat gives the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. That score describes an attack over the network that works without an account or a click from a person on the server, and that is easy to carry out. Apache rates the flaw with a word, critical. The score that CISA, the US cybersecurity agency, added to the official CVE record is 8.1. The difference comes down to one field, the attack complexity, which is set to high in the CISA score. A race condition depends on timing, and getting the timing right takes attempts.

Red Hat makes the same distinction for its own systems. It rates the flaw Critical overall, but Important, one step lower, for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10. On those versions each HTTP/2 stream gets its own part of the program that hands out memory, called a memory allocator, and that makes the flaw harder to exploit. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and older are not affected, and the company notes that HTTP/2 module versions before 2.0.8 do not contain the code with the flaw.

On November 13, the same US agency added its own assessment to the CVE record: no exploitation seen, and not automatable, meaning the attack cannot be reliably run by a script from start to finish.

Apache released version 2.4.71 on November 11, with the corrected line. A day later, the scanning company found 2.4.71 on only about 2,000 hosts. That number says less than it seems, for the same reason as the Ubuntu version numbers. Linux distributions put the fix into their own packages and keep their own version numbers, so a patched Ubuntu or Red Hat server does not announce 2.4.71.

Where the distributions stood when this was written:

  • → Ubuntu published its security notice on November 12, with fixes for 20.04 through 26.10. Ubuntu 20.04 gets its fix through Ubuntu Pro, the paid subscription
  • → The fixed Ubuntu package is 2.4.52-1ubuntu4.27 on 22.04, 2.4.58-1ubuntu8.19 on 24.04 and 2.4.66-2ubuntu2.8 on 26.04
  • → - → Debian fixed version 12 (bookworm) with 2.4.71-1deb12u1, version 13 (trixie) with 2.4.71-1deb13u1, and testing (forky) with 2.4.71-1
  • → Red Hat shipped its first fixes on November 11, the day of Apache’s release, and by November 12 had fixes out for most affected products, with the rest still in progress
  • → Amazon Linux 2 and Amazon Linux 2023 were fixed on November 12

Administrators who built the standalone mod_h2 themselves are in a different position. Its repository has been archived since June 9, 2026, and its last release is 2.0.42, the last version Apache lists as affected. The corrected code only exists in Apache 2.4.71.

On Debian or Ubuntu, the first command below shows whether the HTTP/2 module is loaded, the second shows where Protocols is set, and the third shows the installed package version, to compare with the list above:

1
2
3

sudo apache2ctl -M | grep http2
grep -ri "Protocols" /etc/apache2/
dpkg -l apache2 | grep ^ii

On Red Hat Enterprise Linux and related systems, the company’s bulletin gives these checks. If the first line of the curl answer starts with HTTP/2, the server speaks HTTP/2:

1
2
3

grep http2 /etc/httpd/conf.modules.d/*.conf
grep -ri "Protocols" /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf /etc/httpd/conf.d/*.conf
curl -kI --http2 https://localhost

For a server that cannot take the update yet, the same bulletin gives a way to switch HTTP/2 off. Set the Protocols line to HTTP/1.1 only, in /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf or the file in /etc/httpd/conf.d/ where it is set, and restart the server:

1
2

Protocols http/1.1
sudo systemctl restart httpd

On Debian or Ubuntu, switching the module off does the same, and it also removes the Protocols line that came with it:

1
2

sudo a2dismod http2
sudo systemctl restart apache2

A Protocols line elsewhere that still names h2 does no harm once the module is off, because Apache ignores protocols it cannot provide. Visitors then connect over HTTP/1.1, and the update itself remains the fix.

Run nmap -sV against a server you own and compare the Apache version it announces with the package that is actually installed on it.
